title: What a delegated report is, and why it carries the load
paras: Let's start with what a delegated report is, and why it carries the load. It's the written record where an officer sets out the assessment of an application and the decision — taken under delegated authority, without going to committee. Most authorities delegate the bulk of decisions to officers, keeping committee for the larger, contentious or departure cases. So no committee debate, no members' vote: the report, signed off by a senior officer, is where the reasoning lives, and what's scrutinised if the decision is challenged.

It's a public, legal document — read by the applicant and agent, objectors and supporters, councillors, an inspector on appeal, occasionally a judge. So write it as though they're all looking over your shoulder. A good report reads well to a knowledgeable planner, records the right reasons, and survives an inspector or judge reading it critically; a vague, inconsistent or silent one is a liability, however sound the decision. The citations, section numbers and dates live in the written guide.

One reform to watch. Which decisions must be delegated and which go to committee has always been each authority's own scheme. That's changing: the 2025 planning act provides for a National Scheme of Delegation, setting nationally which categories officers determine and which go to committee. Not in force yet — intended for autumn 2026 — so for now your local scheme governs. The proposed shape: a list that must be officer-determined; a second presumed delegated unless a gateway test is met and a nominated officer and member agree to refer it up; and authority-interest applications to committee, with committees capped at thirteen members. So confirm the current position before assuming an application is yours.

title: The legal frame you are writing inside
paras: Next, the legal frame — three points shaping every report. First, the statutory question: every determination must accord with the development plan unless material considerations indicate otherwise. So the report does two things, in order — establish the development plan position, does the proposal accord with the plan as a whole, then weigh the material considerations pointing the other way. Reach a conclusion without that structure and you're doing the wrong exercise; show the reasoning, don't just land an answer.

Second, the duty to give reasons. For a refusal, and for any condition, the decision notice must give full, clear and precise reasons — straight from your report, so they must follow from the assessment. A grant needs no full statutory reasons on the notice, but don't relax: the report is still the reasoning, public and challengeable, and a common-law duty to give reasons can sometimes arise. Reason a grant as carefully as a refusal. There's a well-known case on the standard — South Bucks — reasons must be intelligible and adequate, and deal with the principal important controversial issues.

Third, how it's judged if challenged. The court doesn't mark it like an exam script — the Mansell principle. Officer reports are written for a knowledgeable readership, not read hypercritically or construed like a statute, and are only unlawful where a defect significantly misleads the decision-maker on something material. Liberating and a warning both: it needn't be perfect, exhaustive or elegant, and a stray typo won't undo the decision — but a material misdirection, misstating a policy, misrepresenting a consultee, ignoring a principal controversial issue, is exactly what will.

title: The anatomy of a report
paras: Now the anatomy. Templates vary but almost all run the same order: facts, then assessment, then a reasoned recommendation. It opens with a header block — reference, site address, a precise description of the development, applicant and agent, ward, case officer, recommendation, date. The description of development matters most: it defines what's being decided and appears on the notice.

Then the facts. Site and surroundings — a short factual description with the constraints: conservation area, listed building, flood zone. The proposal, keyed to the drawings by number. Relevant history — only what bears on the decision, and why: an extant permission or fallback, a previous refusal, a dismissed appeal. Consultations — statutory and non-statutory separated, summarised not reproduced, silence explained. Representations — by theme, number noted but not the measure of weight.

Then policy and constraints — the plan policies that matter, the Framework and guidance, any supplementary documents, ranked not just listed. Then the assessment, the heart of it: the principle of the development, then each principal issue — design and character, residential amenity, highways, heritage, ecology and biodiversity net gain, flood risk, trees, and the rest as needed — with the weight you give each, and why. Then the planning balance and conclusion: the statutory exercise drawn together — plan position, material considerations, whether the tilted balance is engaged, a reasoned conclusion.

Then other matters — human rights, the public sector equality duty, the Community Infrastructure Levy, environmental impact assessment or Habitats screening. And the recommendation and sign-off: approve subject to conditions with their reasons, or refuse with reasons specifying the policies — then case officer and authorising officer.

title: Writing each part well
paras: So how do you write each part well? Keep the facts factual and proportionate — site, proposal and history are description, not argument. Match effort to the case: a householder extension needs no three pages of site description, a strategic scheme does. Don't drown the reader in irrelevant detail like counting every bedroom. And get the description of development exactly right — an inaccurate one causes problems later, at any variation or in enforcement.

Handle representations by weight, not volume. Summarise by theme, not letter by letter; note how many came in, but the number isn't the measure of weight. Separate the statutory consultees, and don't brush aside a statutory consultee's objection without cogent and compelling reasons set out in the report. Distinguish material from non-material — loss of a private view, property value, private disputes — and say briefly why those carry no weight. Don't name individual objectors, and never weight a point by who made it.

Apply the policies, don't just list them. Identify the ones that bear on the decision, which matter most, then apply them to the facts. Use the correct terms of art, especially on heritage: harm to a designated asset — say whether substantial or less than substantial, give it considerable importance and weight under the statutory duty, and run the correct balance; a wrong policy label is the misdirection that undoes a decision. Then make the assessment answer the case — assign weight to the competing considerations and explain it. Work through the principal important controversial issues, the ones the case turns on, not effort spread evenly. And answer the objections' planning points; don't list them then ignore them. Approving despite a dismissed appeal? Explain how the scheme now overcomes the inspector's reasons — consistency is itself a material consideration, and departing from a relevant earlier decision, you must explain why.

Do the balance in the open, as an explicit statutory exercise: state the development plan position as a whole, weigh the material considerations, say whether the presumption in favour of sustainable development is engaged — for instance because relevant policies are out of date — and reach a conclusion a reader can follow. Where a statutory duty or hard test is in play — the heritage duties, or the Habitats Regulations — address it as a threshold before the ordinary balance, not one more item on the scales. And conditions and reasons that stand up: conditions must meet the six tests — necessary, relevant to planning, relevant to the development, enforceable, precise, reasonable — each with a reason. Reasons for refusal must be clear and precise, specify the policies, and follow from the assessment. No boilerplate that doesn't match the findings.

title: The Mansell standard: how your report will be read
paras: Back to the Mansell standard — what a challenge is measured against. It doesn't require perfection, completeness or fine writing. The court assumes an intelligent, informed reader, reads the report fairly and as a whole, and won't pounce on a loose phrase, an omitted detail or a minor error. A report can be workmanlike and still lawful.

What it does require is that the report doesn't significantly mislead the decision-maker on something material — and those failures are predictable. Misstating a policy or applying the wrong test. Misrepresenting a consultee — the classic is a stray "not", reporting it doesn't object when it does. Omitting a principal controversial issue. Failing to address a material consideration the decision turned on, like a real fallback or a statutory heritage or habitats duty. Or carrying an error across by cut-and-paste. None is about style — each could have changed the decision. Write to avoid those and the standard is your friend, not your enemy.

title: Common failings
paras: Now the common failings — the ones a reviewing senior officer, or an inspector, spots at once. Cut-and-paste carryover: the wrong site name, an out-of-date policy number, a consultee response lifted from another case. Policies recited but not applied: a long list, then an assessment that never uses it. Objections described but not answered: summarised at length, then left hanging while the assessment talks about something else.

Then no visible statutory balance — a conclusion without the plan-first, then material-considerations structure. A statutory duty missed — heritage, or the Habitats Regulations, treated as ordinary or not mentioned, when it's really a threshold. Weight given to volume or prominence — counting letters, or leaning on who objected, not the planning points. Effort in the wrong place — pages on the uncontroversial, a paragraph on the issue that decides it. And conditions and reasons that don't match — standard reasons that don't reflect the findings, or conditions that fail the six tests.

title: A working skeleton
paras: A working skeleton to adapt to your template, filling each heading with only what the case needs. Header: reference, address, description of development, applicant and agent, ward, officer, recommendation, date. Then site and surroundings with the constraints; the proposal keyed to the drawings; and relevant history — only what bears, and why.

Then consultations, statutory and non-statutory separated, silence explained. Representations by theme, number noted, material versus non-material flagged. Policy and constraints, ranked, with the Framework, guidance and supplementary planning documents. The assessment — principle first, then each principal issue with weight and reasons, answering the objections. Other matters — human rights, the public sector equality duty, the Community Infrastructure Levy, and environmental impact or Habitats screening.

The planning balance — the statutory exercise drawn together, the tilted balance if engaged, a reasoned conclusion. The recommendation — approve with conditions and reasons, or refuse with reasons specifying the policies. And the sign-off: case officer and authorising officer.

title: The habit that matters most
paras: Finally, the habit that matters most. One discipline underpins all of it: the reasons are the decision. Writing the assessment isn't a chore after deciding; it's how you decide. If you can't articulate, in plain terms, why the benefits outweigh the harms, or why the harm is unacceptable, you haven't finished the assessment — and the answer isn't yet safe.

A junior officer who writes to that standard — the statutory balance in the open, answering the real issues, reasons that would satisfy an inspector — produces decisions that hold up, and learns judgement faster than any amount of reading. The report is where a planner's thinking becomes visible. So make yours worth reading.

This guide covers England, current to July 2026.
